title: Sharding
summary: Split data so one machine is not the hot spot; name the new hot spot you create.

parts.rule: Shard only when one database cannot meet storage or write throughput. Choose a shard key from the dominant access path so ordinary requests route to one shard. Explain routing, rebalancing, hot partitions, cross-shard queries, and failure isolation. Sharding splits responsibility; it does not make uneven traffic or transactions disappear.
parts.why: A good key spreads load while preserving locality for the queries that matter. A poor key turns every read into scatter-gather or sends one large tenant to one overloaded node. Rebalancing a naive hash can move most data when the node count changes, so the lookup scheme is part of the design, not an implementation footnote.
parts.example: A mature URL shortener stores 4 TB and receives more writes than one primary can handle. Redirect is the dominant query and always knows code. Compute logicalBucket = hash(code) % 256, then use a small routing table that maps 256 logical buckets across 8 database primaries, about 32 buckets each. GET /a1b2c3d hashes once, reads the routing entry, and performs a primary-key lookup on one shard. When a ninth primary is added, move selected logical buckets and update the routing map; using hash(code) % 9 directly would remap most codes. Listing links by owner_id no longer has natural locality. Options are an owner-to-codes index partitioned by owner, a separate search view, or a scatter-gather query reserved for rare admin work. State which path earns the extra data copy. A viral code may generate 50,000 reads per second for one row; changing the shard key cannot split a single key, so serve it from cache and replicas. If instead data is sharded by owner_id, one enterprise tenant can become a hot partition and may need dedicated buckets. Keep transactions within a shard where possible, and make the router handle an unavailable shard without pretending the rest of the system is fully healthy.
parts.use: Shard after capacity estimates or measurements show that vertical growth, indexes, caching, and read replicas cannot solve the primary's storage or write limit. Select the key from high-volume queries, use enough logical partitions for future movement, and monitor size and traffic per partition rather than only cluster totals.
parts.refuse: Do not shard a database that comfortably fits on one primary; the operational and query costs are immediate. Avoid a random key that forces every important query to fan out, and do not ignore a tenant or celebrity skew. Hashing does not fix one hot record. Cross-shard joins and transactions should be exceptions with an explicit cost, not the default path.

body:
Rule. Shard only when one database cannot meet storage or write throughput. Choose a shard key from the dominant access path so ordinary requests route to one shard. Explain routing, rebalancing, hot partitions, cross-shard queries, and failure isolation. Sharding splits responsibility; it does not make uneven traffic or transactions disappear.

Why it matters. A good key spreads load while preserving locality for the queries that matter. A poor key turns every read into scatter-gather or sends one large tenant to one overloaded node. Rebalancing a naive hash can move most data when the node count changes, so the lookup scheme is part of the design, not an implementation footnote.

Worked example. A mature URL shortener stores 4 TB and receives more writes than one primary can handle. Redirect is the dominant query and always knows code. Compute logicalBucket = hash(code) % 256, then use a small routing table that maps 256 logical buckets across 8 database primaries, about 32 buckets each. GET /a1b2c3d hashes once, reads the routing entry, and performs a primary-key lookup on one shard. When a ninth primary is added, move selected logical buckets and update the routing map; using hash(code) % 9 directly would remap most codes. Listing links by owner_id no longer has natural locality. Options are an owner-to-codes index partitioned by owner, a separate search view, or a scatter-gather query reserved for rare admin work. State which path earns the extra data copy. A viral code may generate 50,000 reads per second for one row; changing the shard key cannot split a single key, so serve it from cache and replicas. If instead data is sharded by owner_id, one enterprise tenant can become a hot partition and may need dedicated buckets. Keep transactions within a shard where possible, and make the router handle an unavailable shard without pretending the rest of the system is fully healthy.

[[diagram:shards]]

When to use. Shard after capacity estimates or measurements show that vertical growth, indexes, caching, and read replicas cannot solve the primary's storage or write limit. Select the key from high-volume queries, use enough logical partitions for future movement, and monitor size and traffic per partition rather than only cluster totals.

When to refuse. Do not shard a database that comfortably fits on one primary; the operational and query costs are immediate. Avoid a random key that forces every important query to fan out, and do not ignore a tenant or celebrity skew. Hashing does not fix one hot record. Cross-shard joins and transactions should be exceptions with an explicit cost, not the default path.
